text.p: Metals recycler Simsmetal Ltd was likely to consolidate its latest offshore acquisitions in the medium term as attractively priced assets became harder to find.
"That is the issue at the moment, whether we decide to continue growing by acquisition or whether we decide just to organically grow," chief executive officer John Crabb said.

"We have a few things we want to clear up in the short term, acquisitions that may or may not be consummated over the next four or five months, but after that I think we may just rack the cue and consolidate," he told Reuters in an interview.
Simsetal's recent acquisitions in Britain include Dorset-based metals group D.G. Corbin and Sons, while in the U.S. the company is assessing Peck Recycling in Virginia.
U.K. market presence had been improved with the company now holding 12 to 14 percent of the ferrous scrap market in volume terms, he said.

"Our coverage at the moment is quite substantial. We have just put new equipment into London, we have just acquired the Corbin business and we have good coverage in the Midlands through McIntyre. I think it is a matter of building on that base," Crabb said, although he did not rule out further buys.
"If something came up that made sense and offered us incremental benefits we would look at it."

In the U.S. market, the rapid movement of technology had forced the company to look further afield than its West Coast operations, hence the move by its American unit to run the ruler over the Peck Recycling operation in Virginia.

"We decided to move off the West Coast because whether we like it or not, technology transfer is resulting in a lot more scrap consuming capacity coming on line, most of which is in the south and on the east coast," Crabb said.
But he stressed that a purchase price that allowed extra value to be captured remained the key to the Peck or any other acquisition.
"Anybody growing by acquisition must be able to add value to the business. If we do (buy Peck) it will be based on whether we can acquire it at the right price," Crabb said
"My view would be if the price is right then it offers us some opportunities -- if the price is wrong we won't do it."
The purchase price was increasingly a sticking point with the arrival of traders rather than operators pushing vendors' expectations to uneconomic levels, Crabb said.

"The other thing stopping some of our aspirations at the moment is the advent of paper shufflers in this industry, particularly in the U.S. They have pushed the cost of businesses to a level that doesn't make economic sense," he said.
"The expectation of what a business is worth has got past the arithmetic," he said.
